problems.name: Two Sum
problems.description: You are given an array of integers called nums and an integer called target. Return the indices of the two numbers in nums that add up exactly to target. You may assume that each input has exactly one valid answer, and you may not use the same element twice. The order of the two returned indices does not matter.

examples.explanation: The two 3s at indices 0 and 1 sum to 6.

edge_cases: Minimum length array of exactly 2 elements
Duplicate values that together form the answer
Negative numbers combined with positive numbers
Target achieved only by the last two elements
Large magnitude values near the constraint limits

hidden_test_cases.reason: Catches integer overflow when summing large magnitude values
Catches implementations that incorrectly reuse the same index for duplicates
Ensures both indices of an identical pair are returned, not the same index twice

hints: Think about whether you can avoid checking every pair of numbers.
A hash map can let you remember values you've already seen along with their index.
For each number, check whether target minus that number has already appeared in the map before inserting the current number.

solution_approach.key_observation: For every number, the value that would complete the pair is fully determined by target, so we only need a fast way to check if that complement was already seen.
solution_approach.algorithm: Iterate through nums once while maintaining a hash map from value to index. At each index i, compute complement = target - nums[i]. If complement exists in the map, return [map[complement], i]. Otherwise insert nums[i] -> i and continue.
solution_approach.why_it_works: Because we check for the complement before inserting the current value, we never match an element with itself, and every pair is discovered the first time its second element is encountered.
solution_approach.implementation_notes: Insert after checking, not before, to avoid matching an element with itself when target is double that value.

problems.expected_space_complexity: O(n)
problems.what_you_learn: How to use a hash map to reduce pair searching from quadratic to linear time.
common_mistakes: Using nested loops resulting in O(n^2) time when O(n) is expected
Inserting the current value into the map before checking for its complement, causing self-matching
Returning values instead of indices
Assuming the array is sorted when it is not

problems.name: Add Two Numbers
problems.description: You are given two non-empty linked lists representing two non-negative integers. The digits are stored in reverse order, and each node contains a single digit. Add the two numbers and return the sum as a linked list, also in reverse-digit order. You may assume the two numbers do not contain any leading zeros, except the number 0 itself.
constraints: The number of nodes in each list is in the range [1, 100]
It is guaranteed that neither list represents a number with a leading zero, except the number 0 itself

examples.explanation: 342 + 465 = 807, represented in reverse digit order.
9999999 + 9999 = 10009998, represented in reverse digit order with a carry extending the result length.

edge_cases: Both numbers are single digit 0
Lists of different lengths
Sum producing a carry that extends beyond both original list lengths
Sum with no carry at any position
Both lists ending exactly when a final carry needs its own new node

hidden_test_cases.reason: Catches implementations that mishandle a carry that propagates through the longer list's remaining digits
Catches implementations that mishandle a zero-value single-digit operand
Catches implementations that don't correctly propagate a long carry chain across the maximum-length input

hints: Since digits are stored least-significant first, you can add the two lists just like doing addition by hand, from the ones place onward.
Process both lists simultaneously, summing corresponding digits plus any carry from the previous position, and create a new node for each resulting digit (0-9).
Continue as long as either list still has digits remaining, or there's a leftover carry, even after both lists are exhausted.

solution_approach.key_observation: Because digits are already stored in reverse (least-significant-first) order, adding the two linked lists position by position mirrors exactly how manual addition with carry works, without needing to reverse anything first.
solution_approach.algorithm: Create a dummy head node and a tail pointer, and a carry variable initialized to 0. While l1 is non-null, l2 is non-null, or carry is non-zero: sum the current digits of l1 and l2 (using 0 if a list has been exhausted) plus carry; compute the new digit as sum % 10 and update carry = sum / 10; append a new node with the new digit to the result list; advance l1, l2, and the tail pointer as applicable. Return dummy.next.
solution_approach.why_it_works: Processing digit by digit with an explicit carry variable exactly replicates standard addition, and continuing the loop while carry is still non-zero (even after both lists end) correctly handles a final overflow digit.
solution_approach.implementation_notes: Using a dummy head node simplifies list construction by avoiding special-casing the very first result node.

problems.expected_time_complexity: O(max(m, n)) where m, n are the lengths of the two input lists
problems.expected_space_complexity: O(max(m, n)) for the output list (O(1) auxiliary space beyond the output)
problems.what_you_learn: How to combine linked list traversal with arithmetic carry propagation, a pattern applicable to any digit-by-digit computation on linked structures.
common_mistakes: Stopping the loop as soon as either list is exhausted, forgetting to continue processing the longer list's remaining digits
Forgetting to add a final extra node if a carry remains after both lists are fully processed
Not resetting or correctly recomputing carry at each step (carry should be sum / 10 with integer division)
Assuming both lists are the same length, causing index errors or premature termination

problems.name: Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters
problems.description: Given a string s, find the length of the longest substring that does not contain any repeating characters.
constraints: s consists of English letters, digits, symbols, and spaces

examples.explanation: The longest substring without repeating characters is "abc", with length 3.
The longest substring without repeating characters is "b", with length 1.
The longest substring without repeating characters is "wke", with length 3.

edge_cases: Empty string (length 0)
Single character string
String where all characters are identical
String where all characters are already unique
Repeating characters that are far apart in the string

hidden_test_cases.reason: Catches implementations that don't correctly move the window's left boundary forward when a repeat is found further back than expected
Catches implementations that mishandle whitespace as a valid distinct character
Catches implementations that don't correctly finalize the max length after the window is forced to shrink near the end of the string

hints: Think about maintaining a window of characters that are all currently unique.
As you extend the window's right edge, if you encounter a character already inside the window, you need to shrink from the left until that duplicate is removed.
A hash map from character to its most recent index lets you jump the left boundary directly past the previous occurrence instead of shrinking one step at a time.

solution_approach.key_observation: A sliding window that always contains only unique characters can be maintained efficiently by jumping its left boundary directly to just after a repeated character's last seen position, rather than shrinking incrementally.
solution_approach.algorithm: Maintain a hash map from character to its most recent index, and a left pointer starting at 0. For each right pointer from 0 to s.length-1, if s[right] was seen before at an index >= left, move left to (that index + 1). Update the map with s[right] -> right, and track the maximum window size (right - left + 1) seen so far.
solution_approach.why_it_works: By jumping left directly past the conflicting duplicate rather than removing characters one at a time, every character is processed a constant number of times overall, keeping the algorithm linear while still guaranteeing the window has no repeats.
solution_approach.implementation_notes: Always check that the previous occurrence's index is >= left before moving left, since a stale (older, already-excluded) occurrence should not incorrectly shrink the window.

problems.expected_space_complexity: O(min(n, charset size))
problems.what_you_learn: The sliding window technique combined with a hash map for direct left-pointer jumps, a pattern reusable across many substring problems.
common_mistakes: Using a nested loop to check uniqueness at every window, resulting in O(n^2) or O(n^3) time
Forgetting to check whether the previous occurrence's index is within the current window before jumping left, causing left to move backward incorrectly
Off-by-one errors in computing window length (right - left + 1)
Not updating the character's last-seen index after processing, causing stale data on subsequent iterations

problems.name: Median of Two Sorted Arrays
problems.description: Given two sorted arrays nums1 and nums2 of sizes m and n respectively, return the median of the two combined sorted arrays. The overall algorithm should run in O(log(m+n)) time.

examples.explanation: The merged array is [1,2,3], whose median is 2.
The merged array is [1,2,3,4], whose median is the average of 2 and 3, which is 2.5.

edge_cases: One of the two arrays is empty
Both arrays have a single element each
Combined array has an odd total length (median is the single middle element)
Combined array has an even total length (median is the average of the two middle elements)
Arrays of very different sizes, requiring the binary search to always operate on the smaller array

hidden_test_cases.reason: Catches implementations that use an O(m+n) merge-and-find-median approach instead of the required O(log(min(m,n))) binary search partition approach
Catches implementations that don't correctly interleave-partition two evenly matched arrays
Catches implementations that don't correctly handle one completely empty array as a base case within the binary search partition logic

hints: A full merge of the two arrays would take O(m+n) time; think about whether you truly need to merge everything to find just the median.

The median splits the combined array into two equal halves; try binary searching for a partition point in the smaller array such that, combined with a corresponding partition point in the larger array, all elements on the left side are less than or equal to all elements on the right side.

Always perform the binary search on the smaller of the two arrays to guarantee O(log(min(m,n))) time, and use the total combined length's parity to determine whether the median is a single middle value or an average of two.

solution_approach.key_observation: The median can be found by identifying a partition point in each array such that all elements to the left of both partitions (combined) are less than or equal to all elements to the right of both partitions (combined), without ever needing to fully merge or sort the combined data.
solution_approach.algorithm: Ensure nums1 is the smaller array (swap if necessary). Binary search over the partition point i in nums1 (from 0 to m), with the corresponding partition point in nums2 computed as j = (m+n+1)/2 - i. Check the four boundary values (the largest on the left of each partition, and the smallest on the right of each partition). If maxLeftNums1 <= minRightNums2 and maxLeftNums2 <= minRightNums1, the correct partition has been found; compute the median from these four boundary values (accounting for total length parity). If maxLeftNums1 > minRightNums2, decrease i (search a smaller partition in nums1); otherwise increase i.
solution_approach.why_it_works: By binary searching directly on the partition index rather than the values themselves, the algorithm efficiently narrows down to the unique partition point that correctly balances the two halves in sorted order across both arrays simultaneously, achieving logarithmic time relative to the smaller array's size.
solution_approach.implementation_notes: Using sentinel values of positive and negative infinity for out-of-bounds partition boundary lookups (e.g., when i = 0 or i = m) elegantly avoids needing separate conditional logic for these edge cases.

problems.what_you_learn: An advanced binary search technique that searches over a partition index (rather than a value) to solve a problem that superficially seems to require a full merge, achieving a significant complexity improvement.
prerequisites: Merge Two Sorted Lists (as a conceptual O(m+n) baseline comparison)
follow_up_concepts: Kth Smallest Element in a Sorted Matrix
common_mistakes: Fully merging the two arrays and finding the median directly, which is a correct but far slower O(m+n) approach not meeting the required O(log(m+n)) complexity
Binary searching on the larger array instead of the smaller one, potentially causing incorrect boundary calculations or suboptimal time complexity
Forgetting to handle out-of-bounds partition boundaries (when a partition index is 0 or equals the array's full length) using infinity sentinels
Incorrectly computing the corresponding partition index in the second array from the first array's partition index, especially with respect to odd/even total length parity

problems.name: Container With Most Water
problems.description: You are given an integer array height of length n, where height[i] represents the height of a vertical line at position i. Find two lines that, together with the x-axis, form a container that holds the maximum amount of water, and return that maximum area. The container's width is the distance between the two chosen lines' indices, and its height is limited by the shorter of the two lines.

examples.explanation: The lines at indices 1 (height 8) and 8 (height 7) form a container of width 7 and height 7, giving area 49.
The only container available has width 1 and height 1.

edge_cases: Array of exactly two elements
All heights equal
Heights strictly increasing
Heights strictly decreasing
A height of 0 somewhere in the array

hidden_test_cases.reason: Catches implementations that don't correctly compare the current best against a shorter-but-wider container
Catches O(n^2) brute-force implementations that time out on large inputs
Catches implementations that don't correctly handle all-zero heights, which should legitimately produce area 0

hints: Starting with the widest possible container (both ends) and narrowing inward can be more efficient than checking every pair.
At each step, the shorter of the two current lines is the bottleneck limiting area — moving that shorter line's pointer inward is the only way to potentially find a taller container.
Moving the taller line's pointer inward can never help, since width only decreases while height stays capped at the shorter line.

solution_approach.key_observation: For any two pointers, the shorter line determines the container's height, so keeping the taller line fixed and moving the shorter line's pointer inward is the only move that could possibly increase the area; moving the taller pointer can only decrease or maintain area at best.
solution_approach.algorithm: Initialize left = 0 and right = height.length - 1. While left < right, compute the area as (right - left) * min(height[left], height[right]) and update the maximum. Move whichever pointer points to the shorter line inward by one step (left++ if height[left] < height[right], else right--).
solution_approach.why_it_works: By always discarding the shorter line's current position (since it's the limiting bottleneck and can never produce a larger area at that width with any narrower pairing), the two pointers systematically explore all potentially optimal configurations while skipping provably suboptimal ones.
solution_approach.implementation_notes: This greedy two-pointer approach is provably correct because it never discards a pairing that could have been the true maximum; a full proof relies on the bottleneck argument above.

problems.what_you_learn: A greedy two-pointer technique justified by a bottleneck argument, showing how discarding provably suboptimal choices enables linear-time optimization.
common_mistakes: Using an O(n^2) brute-force approach checking every pair of lines
Moving the taller pointer instead of the shorter one, which can never improve the result
Forgetting to update the maximum area before moving a pointer
Off-by-one errors in computing the width (right - left, not right - left + 1, since width is the gap between indices)

problems.name: 3Sum
problems.description: Given an integer array nums, return all unique triplets [nums[i], nums[j], nums[k]] such that i, j, and k are distinct indices and nums[i] + nums[j] + nums[k] equals 0. The solution set must not contain duplicate triplets. The order of the triplets and the order of values within a triplet do not matter.

examples.explanation: These are the only two unique triplets summing to 0.
No triplet sums to 0.
The only triplet available sums to 0.

edge_cases: Array with fewer than 3 non-zero elements
Array where no valid triplet exists
Array containing many duplicate values requiring de-duplication of triplets
Array with all zeros
Array with only positive or only negative values (no valid triplet possible)

hidden_test_cases.reason: Catches implementations that produce duplicate triplets due to inadequate skip-duplicate logic
Catches O(n^3) brute-force implementations that time out at the upper size constraint
Catches implementations that generate the same all-zero triplet multiple times

hints: Sorting the array first can help you use two pointers efficiently and also makes duplicate skipping straightforward.
Fix one element at a time and use two pointers (one from just after it, one from the end) to find pairs that sum to its negation.
After sorting, skip over duplicate values for the fixed element and for the two pointers to avoid generating duplicate triplets.

solution_approach.key_observation: Sorting the array turns the 3-sum problem into, for each fixed first element, a 2-sum-on-sorted-array problem solvable with two pointers, and sorted order also makes duplicate detection trivial via adjacency.
solution_approach.algorithm: Sort nums. For each index i from 0 to n-3, skip if nums[i] equals the previous element (duplicate). If nums[i] > 0, break early since no further triplet can sum to 0. Otherwise, set left = i+1 and right = n-1, and while left < right: compute the sum; if it's 0, record the triplet and move both pointers inward while skipping duplicates; if the sum is less than 0, move left forward; if greater than 0, move right backward.
solution_approach.why_it_works: Fixing the smallest element and using two pointers moving inward on the remaining sorted subarray efficiently explores all complementary pairs in linear time per fixed element, and skipping adjacent duplicates at every level (outer loop and both pointers) guarantees each unique triplet is emitted exactly once.
solution_approach.implementation_notes: The early break when nums[i] > 0 is a valuable optimization since a sorted array's remaining elements can only be >= nums[i], making a zero sum impossible from that point onward.

problems.expected_space_complexity: O(1) extra space excluding the output (O(n log n) or O(n) if the sort implementation requires it internally)
problems.what_you_learn: How sorting combined with two pointers reduces an O(n^3) brute-force triplet search to O(n^2), and how sorted order simplifies duplicate elimination.
common_mistakes: Using a brute-force O(n^3) triple-nested loop instead of the O(n^2) sort-and-two-pointer approach
Forgetting to skip duplicate values for the fixed outer element, producing duplicate triplets
Forgetting to skip duplicate values for the left and right pointers after finding a valid triplet, also producing duplicates
Not sorting the array first, making the two-pointer technique inapplicable

problems.name: Letter Combinations of a Phone Number
problems.description: Given a string digits containing digits from 2 to 9 inclusive, return all possible letter combinations that the number could represent, using the standard telephone keypad mapping (2 -> 'abc', 3 -> 'def', 4 -> 'ghi', 5 -> 'jkl', 6 -> 'mno', 7 -> 'pqrs', 8 -> 'tuv', 9 -> 'wxyz'). Return the combinations in any order. If digits is empty, return an empty list.
constraints: digits[i] is a digit in the range ['2', '9']

examples.explanation: Digit 2 maps to 'abc' and digit 3 maps to 'def', producing all 3*3=9 combinations.
An empty input produces no combinations.
A single digit produces all of its mapped letters as single-character combinations.

edge_cases: Empty string input (return empty list, not a list containing an empty string)
Single digit input
Digit 7 or 9, which map to 4 letters instead of the usual 3
Maximum length input (4 digits) testing full combination generation
All same digit repeated multiple times

hidden_test_cases.reason: Catches implementations that don't correctly handle digits 7 and 9's four-letter mappings alongside standard three-letter digits
Catches implementations that incorrectly return [""] (a list containing an empty string) instead of a truly empty list
Catches implementations that mishandle the case where every digit maps to the maximum 4 letters, at the maximum input length

hints: Think about this as building a string one digit's letter choice at a time.

Use backtracking: at each recursive step, try every letter mapped to the current digit, append it to the string being built, recurse into the next digit, then remove it (backtrack) before trying the next letter.
A complete combination is found once the current string's length equals the number of input digits.

solution_approach.key_observation: Each digit independently contributes one letter to the final combination, so the total set of combinations is the Cartesian product of each digit's possible letters, which backtracking naturally enumerates one digit at a time.
solution_approach.algorithm: If digits is empty, return an empty list immediately. Build a digit-to-letters mapping. Define a recursive backtracking function combine(index, currentString): if index equals digits.length, add currentString to the results and return. Otherwise, for each letter mapped to digits[index], append it to currentString, recursively call combine(index + 1, currentString), then remove the appended letter (backtrack) before trying the next letter.
solution_approach.why_it_works: By exhaustively trying every letter option at each digit position before moving to the next, and backtracking to explore every combination of choices, the recursion naturally generates the complete Cartesian product of all digits' letter options.
solution_approach.implementation_notes: Explicitly checking for an empty digits string upfront avoids an edge case where the recursion would otherwise incorrectly produce a list containing a single empty string instead of a truly empty list.

problems.expected_time_complexity: O(4^n * n) where n is the number of digits (bounded since at most 4 digits are allowed, and each maps to at most 4 letters)
problems.expected_space_complexity: O(4^n * n) for storing all output combinations
problems.what_you_learn: How backtracking naturally computes a Cartesian product across multiple independent choice sets, a pattern generalizable beyond just phone keypad combinations.
common_mistakes: Forgetting to explicitly handle the empty digits string case, returning [""] instead of []
Using an incorrect or incomplete digit-to-letters mapping (especially forgetting that 7 and 9 map to 4 letters, not 3)
Not backtracking correctly (failing to remove the last appended letter before trying the next one), corrupting subsequent combinations
Off-by-one errors in checking when a combination is complete (comparing against digits.length incorrectly)

problems.name: Remove Nth Node From End of List
problems.description: Given the head of a linked list, remove the nth node counting from the end of the list, and return the head of the modified list. You must accomplish this in a single pass through the list.
constraints: The number of nodes in the list is sz

examples.explanation: The 2nd node from the end (value 4) is removed.
The only node is removed, leaving an empty list.
The last node (value 2) is removed.

edge_cases: Removing the only node in a single-node list
Removing the head node itself (n equals the list length)
Removing the tail node (n = 1)
Removing a node in the middle of the list
n exactly equal to the list's total length

hidden_test_cases.reason: Catches implementations that don't correctly handle removing the head when n equals the full list length
Catches implementations that mishandle removing the only node, resulting in an incorrectly non-null returned head
Catches off-by-one errors in the gap between the two pointers when removing a middle node

hints: Think about how to find the nth-from-end node without first counting the total length of the list in a separate pass.
Use two pointers separated by a gap of exactly n nodes: advance the first pointer n steps ahead before starting to move both pointers together.
When the leading pointer reaches the end of the list, the trailing pointer will be positioned just before the node that needs to be removed.

solution_approach.key_observation: Maintaining a fixed gap of n nodes between two pointers means that when the front pointer reaches the end of the list, the back pointer is exactly n nodes from the end, allowing single-pass removal without precomputing list length.
solution_approach.algorithm: Create a dummy node pointing to head to simplify edge cases, and set both fast and slow pointers to dummy. Advance fast n+1 steps ahead. Then move both fast and slow one step at a time until fast becomes null. At this point, slow.next is the node to remove, so set slow.next = slow.next.next. Return dummy.next.
solution_approach.why_it_works: By advancing fast exactly n+1 steps before starting the synchronized walk, the gap between fast and slow ensures that when fast exhausts the list, slow lands precisely on the node just before the target, enabling a direct removal via pointer relinking.
solution_approach.implementation_notes: Using a dummy node handles the special case where the head itself needs to be removed (when n equals the list length) without extra conditional logic.

problems.expected_time_complexity: O(L) where L is the length of the list, achieved in a single pass
problems.what_you_learn: The fixed-gap two-pointer technique for solving 'kth from the end' problems on linked lists in a single traversal.
common_mistakes: Making two separate passes (one to count length, one to remove) instead of the more elegant single-pass two-pointer approach
Not using a dummy node, causing special-case bugs when removing the head node itself
Off-by-one errors in how many steps to advance the fast pointer initially (n vs n+1)
Forgetting to return dummy.next instead of the original (now possibly stale) head reference

All three bracket types are independently matched.
The opening '(' is closed by the wrong bracket type ']'.

Brackets closed in the wrong order
Extra closing bracket with nothing left to match

Catches implementations that mishandle triple nesting order

A stack naturally tracks the most recently opened, still-unclosed bracket.
Push opening brackets, and when you see a closing bracket, it must match the top of the stack; if not, or the stack is empty, the string is invalid.

solution_approach.why_it_works: The stack always holds the currently 'open' brackets in the order they must be closed, so a mismatch or premature empty stack immediately signals invalidity.

problems.name: Merge Two Sorted Lists
problems.description: You are given the heads of two sorted linked lists, list1 and list2. Merge the two lists into a single sorted linked list by splicing together the existing nodes (do not create new nodes), and return the head of the merged list.
constraints: The number of nodes in both lists is in the range [0, 50]
Both list1 and list2 are sorted in non-decreasing order

examples.explanation: The nodes from both lists are interleaved in sorted order.
Both lists are empty, so the merged result is empty.
When one list is empty, the result is simply the other list.

edge_cases: Both lists empty
One list empty, the other non-empty
Lists of very different lengths
Lists with overlapping duplicate values
Lists where all of one list's values are smaller than all of the other's

hidden_test_cases.reason: Catches implementations that don't correctly alternate merging interleaved values
Catches off-by-one bugs when both lists have exactly one equal-valued node
Catches null pointer errors when both inputs are empty

hints: Consider using a dummy head node to simplify edge cases around building the result list.
Compare the current nodes of both lists and attach the smaller one to the result, advancing that list's pointer.
Once one list is exhausted, attach the remainder of the other list directly since it is already sorted.

solution_approach.key_observation: Since both input lists are individually sorted, the smallest unattached node overall is always the smaller of the two lists' current front nodes.
solution_approach.algorithm: Create a dummy node and a tail pointer starting at dummy. After the loop, push the final in-progress interval to the result.

First, add every existing interval that ends before the new interval starts (no overlap, comes entirely before) directly to the result.
Then, merge the new interval with every existing interval that overlaps it, expanding its bounds as needed; finally, add every remaining existing interval that starts after the merged interval ends.

solution_approach.key_observation: Because the input array is already sorted and non-overlapping, a single linear pass can cleanly separate intervals into three groups relative to the new interval: those entirely before it, those overlapping it (which all get merged together), and those entirely after it.

solution_approach.algorithm: Maintain low = 0, mid = 0, high = nums.length - 1. While mid <= high: if nums[mid] == 0, swap nums[low] and nums[mid], increment both low and mid. If nums[mid] == 1, just increment mid. If nums[mid] == 2, swap nums[mid] and nums[high], decrement high (but do not increment mid, since the newly swapped-in value at mid needs to be examined next).
solution_approach.why_it_works: The invariant maintained is that everything before low is 0, everything between low and mid is 1, and everything after high is 2; the region between mid and high is unexamined. This invariant is preserved by each swap/increment operation until mid exceeds high, at which point the entire array is partitioned correctly.
solution_approach.implementation_notes: The asymmetry between the 0-case (advance mid) and 2-case (don't advance mid) is crucial and a common source of bugs; the swapped-in element from the high side must be re-evaluated.

t containing duplicate characters that must all be matched within the window

hints: Think about expanding a window from the right until it contains all required characters, then shrinking it from the left as much as possible while it remains valid.

Maintain a frequency map of required characters from t, and a count of how many distinct required characters are currently 'satisfied' (present in the window with sufficient count) as you expand and shrink.

Whenever the window becomes valid (all required characters satisfied), try shrinking from the left to find the tightest valid window before continuing to expand, recording the best (shortest) window found throughout.

solution_approach.key_observation: A sliding window that expands to satisfy all required character counts and then greedily shrinks from the left while remaining valid will, across the entire scan, encounter every candidate minimal window, since any shorter valid window would have to be discovered during some shrink phase.
solution_approach.algorithm: Build a frequency map (required) of characters needed from t, and track requiredCount (the number of distinct characters still needed). Maintain a window frequency map and two pointers left and right. Expand right across s, updating the window's frequency map; whenever a character's window count reaches its required count for the first time, decrement requiredCount. Whenever requiredCount reaches 0 (window is fully valid), try shrinking left as far as possible while the window remains valid, updating the best (minimum) window found at each valid shrink step, and incrementing requiredCount again when a required character's count drops below what's needed.
solution_approach.why_it_works: Because the window only ever shrinks while it remains valid, and expands otherwise, every minimal valid window ending at some right boundary is captured at the moment just before it would become invalid from further shrinking, ensuring the global minimum is found across the single combined pass.
solution_approach.implementation_notes: Only decrementing/incrementing requiredCount when a character's count crosses its required threshold (rather than on every single frequency update) keeps the validity check itself O(1) rather than requiring a full frequency map comparison at every step.

Larger array testing exponential growth up to the constraint's maximum (2^10 = 1024 subsets)

hints: Think about building subsets incrementally: for each element, you have exactly two choices — include it in the current subset, or don't.
Use backtracking: at each index, first record the current subset as one valid result, then recursively try adding each subsequent element one at a time.
Alternatively, you can generate all subsets iteratively by starting with just the empty subset and, for each new number, adding it to every subset generated so far.

solution_approach.key_observation: Every subset corresponds to a unique choice of include/exclude for each element, so systematically exploring these binary choices via backtracking (or equivalently, doubling the subset list for each new element) generates the complete power set without duplication.
solution_approach.algorithm: Define a recursive backtracking function that takes a starting index and the current subset being built. First, add a copy of the current subset to the results list (representing 'stop growing here'). Then, for each index i from the starting index to the end of nums, add nums[i] to the current subset, recursively call the function with startIndex = i + 1, and then remove nums[i] from the current subset (backtrack) before trying the next index.
solution_approach.why_it_works: By recording the subset at every recursive call (not just at a fixed depth) and always moving the starting index strictly forward before each recursive branch, every distinct combination of included elements is generated exactly once, since no element can ever be reconsidered once skipped past.
solution_approach.implementation_notes: The iterative doubling approach (for each new number, duplicate all existing subsets and add the number to each duplicate) is a simpler-to-implement, equally valid alternative to full backtracking.

problems.expected_space_complexity: O(2^n * n) for storing all subsets in the output
problems.what_you_learn: The foundational backtracking pattern for generating all subsets (the power set) of a set, directly applicable to a wide range of combinatorial enumeration problems.

The letters S-E-E can be traced through adjacent cells starting from a different part of the grid.
Although A-B-C can be traced, reaching a second B would require reusing an already-used cell, which is not allowed.

edge_cases: Single cell grid matching a single-character word
Word longer than the total number of cells in the grid (impossible, false)
Word that revisits the same cell if reuse were allowed (must correctly return false)
Word matching a path that wraps around in a non-straight-line shape

hidden_test_cases.reason: Catches implementations that don't correctly restore visited state (fail to backtrack), causing incorrect false negatives on long valid paths, or performance issues from not pruning failed branches early

hints: Think of this as a DFS/backtracking search starting from every possible cell that matches the word's first character.
As you extend the path to match subsequent characters, mark the current cell as 'in use' (e.g., by temporarily altering its value) so it can't be revisited within the same path attempt.
If a path attempt fails partway through, backtrack by restoring the cell's original value before trying a different direction or starting position.

solution_approach.key_observation: Because a cell cannot be reused within a single word path, marking cells as temporarily 'visited' during the DFS and restoring them upon backtracking correctly enforces this constraint while still allowing the same cell to be revisited in a different, unrelated path attempt.
solution_approach.algorithm: For each cell (r, c) in the grid matching word[0], start a DFS/backtracking search dfs(r, c, index). If board[r][c] does not match word[index], return false. If index equals word.length - 1, return true (the full word has been matched). Otherwise, temporarily mark board[r][c] as visited (e.g., replace it with a sentinel character), recursively try all four neighboring directions with dfs(neighborRow, neighborCol, index + 1), and restore board[r][c] to its original value afterward regardless of the recursive outcome. Return true if any starting cell and direction sequence succeeds.
solution_approach.why_it_works: Temporarily marking a cell during the current path attempt and always restoring it afterward (backtracking) ensures cells are correctly excluded only while genuinely part of the in-progress path, allowing the algorithm to correctly explore all other independent path possibilities without permanently consuming any cell.
solution_approach.implementation_notes: Adding an early pruning check (verifying the first character exists somewhere in the board, or checking character frequency counts against the board's overall letter frequency) can significantly speed up cases where the word clearly cannot be found.

problems.expected_space_complexity: O(L) for the recursion stack, where L is the length of word
problems.what_you_learn: The grid backtracking pattern combining DFS exploration with in-place visited marking and restoration, widely applicable to path-finding problems on 2D grids with a no-reuse constraint.

examples.explanation: The largest rectangle has height 5 and width 2 (spanning bars at indices 2 and 3), giving area 10.
The largest rectangle uses just the bar of height 4 alone (width 1), or equivalently both bars at height 2 (width 2); 4 is the maximum.

edge_cases: Single bar (area is simply that bar's height)
All bars the same height (the largest rectangle spans the entire histogram)
Strictly increasing heights
Strictly decreasing heights
A bar of height 0 splitting the histogram into independent sections

hints: For each bar, think about the largest rectangle that could use that bar's height as its limiting (shortest) height — this requires knowing how far it can extend left and right before hitting a shorter bar.
A monotonic increasing stack of bar indices can efficiently determine, for each bar, the nearest shorter bar to its left and right in a single pass.

When a new bar is shorter than the bar at the top of the stack, that means the top bar's rectangle can no longer extend further right — pop it and calculate its maximum rectangle area using the current index as its right boundary and the new stack top as its left boundary.

solution_approach.key_observation: For each bar, the largest rectangle using that bar's height as the limiting height extends as far left and right as possible until hitting a shorter bar on either side, and a monotonic increasing stack can efficiently determine both boundaries for every bar in a single linear pass.
solution_approach.algorithm: Maintain a stack of indices representing bars with increasing heights, and iterate through heights with an added sentinel bar of height 0 at the very end to force final flushing of the stack. For each index i (including the final sentinel), while the stack is non-empty and heights[i] < heights[stack.top()], pop index j from the stack; compute the width as (i - stack.top() - 1) if the stack is non-empty after popping, or i if the stack is now empty (meaning bar j extends all the way from the beginning); compute area = heights[j] * width and update the maximum area. Push i onto the stack after the while loop.
solution_approach.why_it_works: When a shorter bar is encountered, every taller bar still on the stack can no longer extend rightward past the current position, so popping and finalizing their rectangle area at that moment correctly captures their maximum possible extent; the new stack top after popping represents the nearest bar shorter than the popped one, correctly establishing its left boundary.
solution_approach.implementation_notes: Appending a sentinel height of 0 at the end of the array (conceptually, without modifying the actual input) ensures every remaining bar on the stack gets properly popped and evaluated by the end of the pass, rather than requiring separate cleanup logic after the main loop.

problems.expected_space_complexity: O(n) for the stack in the worst case

problems.name: Decode Ways
problems.description: A message containing letters A through Z is encoded using the mapping 'A' -> 1, 'B' -> 2, ..., 'Z' -> 26. Given a string s containing only digits, return the number of ways to decode it back into letters. If the string cannot be decoded at all (contains an invalid encoding), return 0.
constraints: s consists of only digits and may contain leading zeros

examples.explanation: "12" can be decoded as "AB" (1 2) or "L" (12).
"226" can be decoded as "BZ" (2 26), "VF" (22 6), or "BBF" (2 2 6).
"06" cannot be decoded since a leading zero never corresponds to any valid single-digit letter mapping (0 has no letter, and "06" isn't a valid two-digit code either).

edge_cases: String starting with '0' (immediately 0 ways, since no valid decoding can start with 0)
String containing a lone '0' digit anywhere that can't be paired with the preceding digit to form 10 or 20
String of all identical non-zero digits (testing exponential-looking but polynomial DP growth)
Two-digit substring exceeding 26 (only decodable as two separate single digits, not one combined digit)
String consisting of a single digit

hidden_test_cases.reason: Catches implementations that don't correctly propagate a 0 immediately following a digit that can't validly pair with it (here, '0' after '1' can only combine as '10', constraining the rest)

Catches implementations that incorrectly treat '30' as decodable, when 30 exceeds the valid two-digit range (10-26) and '0' alone is also never valid

hints: Think about how the number of ways to decode the string up to position i relates to decoding up to positions i-1 and i-2.

At each position, you can decode using just the single current digit (if it's not '0'), extending the count of ways from one position back, or using the current digit combined with the previous one as a two-digit code (if that two-digit value is between 10 and 26), extending the count of ways from two positions back.
Define dp[i] as the number of ways to decode the prefix of length i, with dp[0] = 1 (empty prefix has exactly one, trivial, way to decode) as the base case.

solution_approach.key_observation: The number of ways to decode a prefix ending at position i is the sum of the ways to decode using the single last digit (if valid, i.e., not '0') plus the ways to decode using the last two digits combined (if that two-digit number falls between 10 and 26 inclusive).
solution_approach.algorithm: Create a DP array of size s.length + 1, with dp[0] = 1 (base case for the empty prefix) and dp[1] = 1 if s[0] != '0' else 0. For each position i from 2 to s.length: if s[i-1] != '0', add dp[i-1] to dp[i] (using the single last digit as a valid one-digit code). If the two-digit number formed by s[i-2] and s[i-1] is between 10 and 26 inclusive, add dp[i-2] to dp[i] (using the last two digits as a valid two-digit code). Return dp[s.length].
solution_approach.why_it_works: Every valid decoding of the prefix ending at position i must end with either a single-digit code or a two-digit code as its very last decoded letter, and summing the ways achievable through each of these two mutually exclusive possibilities (when valid) correctly counts every distinct decoding.
solution_approach.implementation_notes: Careful handling of '0' is essential throughout: a lone '0' is never independently decodable, and a '0' can only be validly consumed as the second digit of a two-digit code between 10 and 20 (since '0' as the tens digit like '05' or as a standalone digit is never valid).

hints: Distinguish between two related but different questions at each node: 'what's the best path sum if I can only continue upward from here into my parent' versus 'what's the best path sum using this node as the highest point (peak) of the path'.

A subtree can only contribute its value to a path continuing into the parent if that contribution is added to at most one of its own children's best single-direction contributions (not both, since a path can't branch).

At every node, compute the best single-direction contribution (for returning to the parent) while separately checking whether using both children's contributions plus the current node's value (peaking at this node) would be a new global maximum.

solution_approach.key_observation: A path can bend at most once (at its single highest point), so while recursing, each node can only pass a single-direction (one child's worth) contribution up to its parent, but can still separately consider combining both children's contributions locally to check if peaking at itself yields a new global maximum.
solution_approach.algorithm: Maintain a globalMax variable initialized to negative infinity. Define a recursive function maxContribution(node): if node is null, return 0. Recursively compute leftContribution = max(0, maxContribution(node.left)) and rightContribution = max(0, maxContribution(node.right)) (clamping negative contributions to 0, since a negative contribution should simply be excluded from the path rather than dragging down the sum). Update globalMax = max(globalMax, node.val + leftContribution + rightContribution) (considering this node as the path's peak, using both children). Return node.val + max(leftContribution, rightContribution) (the single-direction contribution usable by this node's own parent). After the initial call from the root, return globalMax.
solution_approach.why_it_works: By clamping negative contributions to 0, only genuinely beneficial subtree paths are ever included; by separately tracking a global maximum that considers combining both children (which a valid path can do only at its single peak node) versus a returned value that only ever uses one child (since a path continuing further up cannot branch), the recursion correctly explores every possible path shape in the tree exactly once.
solution_approach.implementation_notes: It's crucial that the value returned to the parent (for chaining) uses only the max of the two children's contributions, while the value used to update globalMax can use the sum of both, since these represent genuinely different structural roles (continuing a path vs. being the path's peak).

solution_approach.key_observation: In a list with a cycle, a faster-moving pointer will eventually lap a slower-moving pointer and they will meet at the same node; in an acyclic list, the faster pointer simply reaches the end.
solution_approach.algorithm: Initialize slow and fast pointers both at head. Loop while fast and fast.next are not null: move slow one step and fast two steps. If slow and fast ever point to the same node, return true. If the loop exits because fast or fast.next is null, return false.

solution_approach.implementation_notes: Always check fast != null and fast.next != null before advancing fast to avoid a null pointer dereference.

Updating the value of an existing key (should not count as a new insertion for eviction purposes, and should mark it as most recently used)

Repeated get calls on the same key not causing incorrect eviction order
hints: A hash map alone gives O(1) lookup but doesn't track usage order; a plain array or list gives ordering but not O(1) access.
Combine a hash map (for O(1) key lookup) with a doubly linked list (for O(1) reordering and eviction) where the hash map stores key -> node reference.
Keep the most recently used node near one end of the list and the least recently used near the other; every get or put should move the accessed node to the 'most recently used' end.

solution_approach.key_observation: A hash map provides O(1) key-to-node lookup, while a doubly linked list allows O(1) removal and re-insertion of a node at either end without shifting other elements, and combining both structures satisfies every required operation in O(1).
solution_approach.algorithm: Maintain a hash map from key to doubly linked list node, and a doubly linked list with dummy head and tail sentinels, ordered from most-recently-used (near head) to least-recently-used (near tail). get(key): if key exists, move its node to just after the head (mark as most recently used) and return its value; otherwise return -1. put(key, value): if key exists, update its value and move it to just after the head. Otherwise, if at capacity, remove the node just before the tail (least recently used) from both the list and the map; then insert a new node for the key just after the head and add it to the map.
solution_approach.why_it_works: Because the doubly linked list supports O(1) removal (given a direct node reference from the hash map) and O(1) insertion at a known position, every access or update can reposition a node to the 'most recently used' end in constant time, and eviction always targets the correct end of the list.
solution_approach.implementation_notes: Using dummy head and tail sentinel nodes (rather than null checks) significantly simplifies the insertion and removal logic by eliminating edge cases for an empty or single-element list.

problems.expected_time_complexity: O(1) average time for both get and put
problems.expected_space_complexity: O(capacity)
problems.what_you_learn: How combining a hash map with a doubly linked list achieves O(1) operations for a data structure requiring both fast lookup and fast reordering, a foundational systems-design pattern.

problems.description: Evaluate the value of an arithmetic expression given in Reverse Polish Notation (postfix notation). Valid operators are +, -, *, and /. Each operand may be an integer or another expression's result. Division between two integers should truncate toward zero. The input is guaranteed to represent a valid arithmetic expression with no division by zero.

hints: Postfix notation naturally lends itself to processing with a stack.
Scan the tokens left to right: push numbers onto the stack, and when you see an operator, pop the two most recent operands to apply it.
Pay close attention to the order of the popped operands for subtraction and division, since these operations are not commutative — the second-popped value should be the left-hand operand.

solution_approach.key_observation: In postfix notation, an operator always immediately follows its two operands in the token stream, so a stack naturally accumulates operands and resolves them the moment an operator is encountered.
solution_approach.algorithm: Initialize an empty stack. For each token: if it's a number, push it onto the stack. If it's an operator, pop the top two values (call them b then a, since b was pushed most recently), compute a OP b according to the operator, and push the result back onto the stack. After processing all tokens, the single remaining value on the stack is the final result.
solution_approach.why_it_works: Because postfix guarantees operators appear only after their operands are fully resolved, always applying an operator to the two most recently computed/pushed values correctly reconstructs the intended expression tree evaluation order.
solution_approach.implementation_notes: For division, use truncation toward zero (as in most languages' integer division for positive results, but requiring explicit handling for negative results in languages that floor instead of truncate).

problems.expected_space_complexity: O(n) for the stack in the worst case
problems.what_you_learn: How postfix (Reverse Polish) notation eliminates the need for parentheses and operator precedence rules, and how a stack directly implements its evaluation.

hints: Unlike Maximum Subarray (sum-based), multiplying by a negative number can flip a very small (very negative) product into the largest positive product — this means you need to track more than just a running maximum.

At each position, maintain both a running maximum product and a running minimum product ending at that position, since a large negative minimum could become the new maximum when multiplied by another negative number.

At each step, compute the candidates (current number alone, current number * previous max, current number * previous min), and the new max and min are the largest and smallest of these three candidates respectively.

solution_approach.key_observation: Because multiplying two negative numbers produces a positive result, the most negative product ending at the previous position could become the most positive product after multiplying by another negative number, so both a running maximum and a running minimum must be tracked simultaneously.
solution_approach.algorithm: Initialize maxProd = nums[0], minProd = nums[0], and result = nums[0]. For each subsequent number n in nums: compute the three candidates n, n * maxProd, and n * minProd; set the new maxProd to the largest of these three candidates, and the new minProd to the smallest of these three candidates. Update result = max(result, maxProd) after each step. Return result.
solution_approach.why_it_works: By tracking both extremes (max and min) at every position, the algorithm correctly accounts for sign flips: a very negative running product (minProd) can, upon multiplying by a new negative number, become the new best (maximum) product, which a single running-maximum-only approach (as in Maximum Subarray) would have discarded prematurely.
solution_approach.implementation_notes: Computing all three candidates before updating both maxProd and minProd (rather than updating one and then using its new value to compute the other) is essential to avoid using a value that's already been overwritten in the same iteration.

problems.what_you_learn: How multiplication's sign-flipping behavior requires tracking dual running extremes (both max and min) rather than a single running best, extending the Kadane's Algorithm idea from Maximum Subarray.

If the middle element is greater than the rightmost element, the minimum must be to the right of mid; otherwise it's at mid or to the left.

You can detect a cycle using DFS with node coloring (unvisited, currently-in-progress, fully-visited), or using Kahn's algorithm (BFS-based topological sort tracking in-degrees).

solution_approach.algorithm: Build an adjacency list representing the graph. Using Kahn's algorithm: compute the in-degree of every node, and initialize a queue with all nodes having in-degree 0. Replace one character within a window like "ABBA" to get "BBBB" or similar, giving length 4.

A window of size L is valid if L minus the count of its most frequent character is at most k; expand the window and shrink from the left only when this condition is violated.

solution_approach.key_observation: Within any window, replacing every character except the most frequent one costs (window length - max frequency count) replacements, so a window is achievable exactly when this quantity is at most k.
solution_approach.algorithm: Maintain a sliding window [left, right] and a frequency count array for the 26 letters. Expand right one step at a time, updating the frequency count and a running maxFreq (the highest frequency count seen in any window state so far). As you compute the height of each subtree recursively, also track the best diameter (left height + right height) seen at any node.
Use a variable outside the recursive height function to record the maximum left+right sum encountered across all nodes, and return that as the final answer.

solution_approach.key_observation: The longest path through any given node equals the height of its left subtree plus the height of its right subtree, and the true diameter is the maximum of this quantity over every node in the tree, not just the root.

Alternatively, use a Union-Find (Disjoint Set Union) structure: union connected cities together, and count the number of distinct root/representative groups at the end.

solution_approach.algorithm: Initialize a Union-Find structure with n separate sets, one per city. For every pair (i, j) where isConnected[i][j] == 1, union the sets containing i and j. After processing the entire matrix, count the number of distinct root representatives remaining across all n cities — this count is the number of provinces.
solution_approach.why_it_works: Union-Find directly and efficiently merges cities known to be connected into the same set, and because union operations are transitive (if A merges with B and B merges with C, A and C end up in the same set), the final distinct root count accurately reflects the true number of connected components, honoring both direct and indirect connections.
solution_approach.implementation_notes: Using both path compression (flattening the tree during find operations) and union by rank/size keeps each operation nearly constant time on average, making the overall algorithm very efficient even as n grows.

No contiguous substring of s2 is a rearrangement of "ab".

Consider sliding a fixed-size window (the length of s1) across s2, comparing frequency counts at each position.
Instead of recomputing the frequency comparison from scratch at every window position, update counts incrementally as the window slides (add the new right character, remove the old left character).

Compare them; if equal, return true. Then slide the window one character at a time across the rest of s2: add the new rightmost character's count and remove the old leftmost character's count, comparing frequency arrays after each slide.
solution_approach.why_it_works: Since a permutation is defined purely by character frequency (order doesn't matter), matching frequency counts within a fixed-size window is both necessary and sufficient to detect a permutation of s1 at that window position.
solution_approach.implementation_notes: Instead of comparing full 26-length arrays at every step (O(26) per step), maintaining a single 'number of matching character counts' counter that increments/decrements incrementally can reduce the per-step cost to O(1).

problems.description: You are given an array of characters tasks representing CPU tasks (each letter represents a different task type), and an integer n representing the cooldown period between two tasks of the same type. examples.explanation: One valid order is A,B,idle,A,B,idle,A,B, taking 8 total time units.
With no cooldown required, all 6 tasks can run back to back.
The task A dominates, requiring idle slots to be filled by other tasks or forced idle time to satisfy its own cooldown.

edge_cases: n = 0 (no cooldown needed, answer is simply the total number of tasks)
Single task type repeated many times (idle time dominates)
All tasks distinct (no cooldown constraint ever binds, answer is just total task count)
One task type occurring far more frequently than all others combined
Multiple task types tied for the highest frequency

hidden_test_cases.reason: Catches implementations that don't correctly compute the idle-time formula at scale or use an inefficient simulation approach that would time out

hints: Focus on the task type(s) with the highest frequency, since they impose the most restrictive scheduling constraint.
Imagine arranging time into 'blocks' anchored by the most frequent task, each block being (n+1) units long, with idle slots filled by other tasks where possible.
The answer is the maximum of the total number of tasks and a formula based on the most frequent task's count, the number of tasks tied for that maximum frequency, and the cooldown period n.

solution_approach.key_observation: The scheduling is fundamentally constrained by the most frequent task type: it requires (maxFreq - 1) cooldown gaps of size n after each of its occurrences except the last, and other tasks (including those also at maxFreq) fill into those gaps as much as possible, but if there are enough distinct tasks overall, no idle time is needed at all.
solution_approach.algorithm: Count the frequency of each task type. Find maxFreq (the highest frequency among all task types) and maxCount (the number of distinct task types that share this maxFreq). Compute the idle-time-based formula: (maxFreq - 1) * (n + 1) + maxCount. The final answer is the maximum of this formula's result and the total number of tasks (tasks.length), since if there are enough other tasks to fill every gap, no additional idle time beyond the plain task count is ever needed.
solution_approach.why_it_works: The most frequent task creates maxFreq - 1 mandatory gaps of size n between its occurrences (plus one slot for each of its own occurrences and any other tasks tied for that same max frequency, which must also be spread across those final slots); when there are enough other distinct tasks to completely fill these gaps, the true lower bound instead becomes simply the total task count, which the max() with tasks.length correctly captures.
solution_approach.implementation_notes: This is a purely mathematical/greedy formula requiring no actual simulation of the schedule, making it extremely efficient; a heap-based simulation approach is also valid but unnecessary for computing just the final count.

2 does not exist in nums, so -1 is returned.

hints: Since the array is sorted, you can eliminate half the remaining search space with each comparison.
Maintain a left and right boundary and repeatedly check the middle element.
If the middle element is less than target, search the right half; if greater, search the left half; if equal, you've found it.

solution_approach.key_observation: Sorted order allows a single comparison at the midpoint to determine which half of the array could possibly contain the target, discarding the other half entirely.
solution_approach.algorithm: Initialize left = 0, right = nums.length - 1. While left <= right, compute mid = left + (right - left) / 2. If nums[mid] == target, return mid. If nums[mid] < target, set left = mid + 1. Otherwise set right = mid - 1. If the loop ends, return -1.
solution_approach.why_it_works: Each iteration halves the search space based on sorted order, guaranteeing the target (if present) is always still within the [left, right] bounds until it's found or the range becomes empty.
solution_approach.implementation_notes: Computing mid as left + (right - left) / 2 instead of (left + right) / 2 avoids potential integer overflow on very large arrays.

hints: This is a classic single-source shortest path problem on a weighted directed graph — think about which well-known algorithm is designed exactly for this.
Dijkstra's algorithm uses a min-heap (priority queue) to always process the currently-known closest unvisited node next, updating (relaxing) the distances to its neighbors.

After computing the shortest distance from k to every other node, the answer is the maximum of all these shortest distances (since the signal must reach everyone, the last one to be reached determines the total time); if any node is still unreachable (infinite distance), return -1.

solution_approach.key_observation: The problem asks for the time until the signal reaches every node, which is exactly the maximum over all nodes of their shortest-path distance from k, computable efficiently using Dijkstra's algorithm since all edge weights are non-negative.
solution_approach.algorithm: Build an adjacency list representation of the graph from times. Initialize a distances array/map with infinity for all nodes except distances[k] = 0. Use a min-heap initialized with (0, k). While the heap is non-empty, extract the node with the smallest current known distance; if this distance is greater than the already-recorded distance for that node, skip it (stale entry). Otherwise, for each neighbor via an outgoing edge, compute the candidate new distance (current distance + edge weight); if it's less than the neighbor's currently known distance, update it and push (newDistance, neighbor) onto the heap. After the heap is exhausted, find the maximum distance among all n nodes; if any node still has distance infinity, return -1, otherwise return that maximum.
solution_approach.why_it_works: Dijkstra's algorithm greedily finalizes the shortest distance to the closest unvisited node at each step, which is correct because all edge weights are non-negative (so no shorter path could ever be found later through a node with a currently larger tentative distance); the heap ensures the closest unprocessed node is always considered next in O(log V) time per extraction.
solution_approach.implementation_notes: Skipping 'stale' heap entries (where the extracted distance no longer matches the currently best known distance for that node, because it was already improved via a different path since being pushed) is a standard and important optimization/correctness detail in heap-based Dijkstra implementations.

problems.expected_time_complexity: O(E log V) where V is the number of nodes and E is the number of edges, using a heap-based Dijkstra implementation
problems.expected_space_complexity: O(V + E) for the adjacency list, distances array, and heap
problems.what_you_learn: Dijkstra's algorithm, the foundational technique for single-source shortest path computation on weighted graphs with non-negative edge weights, widely applicable across network and routing problems.

problems.name: Koko Eating Bananas
problems.description: Koko loves bananas and has n piles of bananas, where piles[i] is the number of bananas in pile i. Koko can decide an eating speed of k bananas per hour. Each hour, she chooses one pile and eats up to k bananas from it (if the pile has fewer than k bananas, she finishes that pile for the hour and does not eat from another pile that same hour). Koko wants to finish eating all the bananas within h hours. Return the minimum integer eating speed k such that she can finish all piles within h hours.

examples.explanation: At speed 4, Koko takes ceil(3/4)+ceil(6/4)+ceil(7/4)+ceil(11/4) = 1+2+2+3 = 8 hours, exactly meeting the limit.
With only 5 hours and 5 piles, she must finish each pile in a single hour, so speed must cover the largest pile.
With one extra hour available, a slightly lower speed of 23 suffices.

edge_cases: h exactly equal to the number of piles (must finish each pile in one hour, so speed = max pile)
h much larger than the number of piles (very slow speed of 1 may suffice)
Single pile array
All piles the same size
Very large pile sizes near the constraint maximum

hidden_test_cases.reason: Catches integer overflow when summing hours across very large pile sizes and speeds

Re-verifies exact boundary case where the computed hours exactly equal h, not less

hints: Instead of searching over the piles directly, think about searching over the possible eating speeds themselves.
For any candidate speed k, you can compute exactly how many hours are needed by summing ceil(pile / k) for every pile — and this hours-needed function decreases as k increases.
Binary search over k from 1 to the maximum pile size, checking the hours-needed function's monotonic behavior to find the smallest valid k.

solution_approach.key_observation: The total hours required is a non-increasing function of the eating speed k, so instead of searching the piles, you can binary search directly over the space of possible speeds to find the minimum one that meets the hour limit.
solution_approach.algorithm: Set low = 1 and high = max(piles). While low < high: compute mid = low + (high - low) / 2, then compute hoursNeeded by summing ceil(pile / mid) over all piles. If hoursNeeded <= h, this speed works, so try smaller: high = mid. Otherwise it's too slow, so low = mid + 1. Return low (or high) as the minimum valid speed.
solution_approach.why_it_works: Because increasing speed can only decrease or maintain the hours needed, the set of valid speeds forms a contiguous range starting from some minimum value up to infinity, which is exactly the monotonic structure binary search requires to find that boundary.
solution_approach.implementation_notes: Compute ceil(pile / mid) using integer arithmetic as (pile + mid - 1) / mid to avoid floating point precision issues.

problems.what_you_learn: Binary search on the answer space itself (rather than on array indices), a powerful technique for optimization problems with a monotonic feasibility condition.

Using floating-point division instead of integer ceiling division, causing precision errors
Integer overflow when summing hours across many large piles with a small speed
Off-by-one errors in the binary search boundaries (using high = mid - 1 instead of high = mid when mid is a valid candidate)

problems.name: Rotting Oranges
problems.description: You are given an m x n grid where each cell can have one of three values: 0 representing an empty cell, 1 representing a fresh orange, or 2 representing a rotten orange. Every minute, any fresh orange that is adjacent (horizontally or vertically) to a rotten orange becomes rotten. Return the minimum number of minutes that must elapse until no cell has a fresh orange. If this is impossible, return -1.

examples.explanation: The rot spreads outward minute by minute from the initial rotten orange, taking 4 minutes to reach every fresh orange.
The orange in the bottom-left corner is isolated by zeros and can never become rotten.
There are no fresh oranges at all, so 0 minutes are needed.

edge_cases: No fresh oranges at all (0 minutes needed immediately)
No rotten oranges but fresh oranges exist (impossible, return -1)
Fresh orange completely isolated by empty cells (impossible, return -1)
Grid with multiple initially rotten oranges spreading simultaneously
Single cell grid

hidden_test_cases.reason: Catches implementations that process one rotten source at a time (sequential BFS) instead of all sources simultaneously (true multi-source BFS), producing an incorrect (too large) minute count
Catches implementations that mishandle a grid with no oranges at all
Catches implementations that don't correctly detect the impossible case when there are fresh oranges but zero rotten oranges to start the spread

hints: Think of every initially rotten orange as a simultaneous starting point for a spreading process.
A multi-source BFS, where all rotten oranges are enqueued at the very start (minute 0), naturally models rot spreading outward one 'ring' of adjacency per minute.
After the BFS completes, check whether any fresh oranges remain unreached; if so, the answer is -1, otherwise it's the number of minutes (BFS levels) processed.

solution_approach.key_observation: Because all rotten oranges spread simultaneously each minute, a multi-source BFS (enqueuing every initially rotten orange at once, rather than running separate BFS for each) directly models the simultaneous spread and lets each processed level correspond exactly to one elapsed minute.
solution_approach.algorithm: Scan the grid, enqueueing the coordinates of every initially rotten orange and counting the total number of fresh oranges. Perform level-order BFS: for each level (minute), dequeue all currently queued rotten oranges, and for each of their fresh neighbors, mark them rotten, decrement the fresh count, and enqueue them for the next level. Increment a minutes counter after each level that actually rotted at least one new orange. After BFS completes, if freshCount is 0, return the minutes counter; otherwise return -1.
solution_approach.why_it_works: Since all currently-rotten oranges are processed together within a single BFS level, exactly one minute of simultaneous spreading is modeled per level, and any fresh orange left unreached after the BFS terminates is provably unreachable (isolated), correctly triggering the -1 case.
solution_approach.implementation_notes: Take care to only increment the minutes counter for levels where new oranges actually rotted, to avoid overcounting when the BFS queue becomes empty exactly as the last level exhausts fresh neighbors.

problems.expected_space_complexity: O(m * n) for the BFS queue in the worst case
problems.what_you_learn: How multi-source BFS naturally models simultaneous, parallel spreading processes, with each BFS level corresponding directly to one unit of elapsed time.
common_mistakes: Running separate BFS traversals for each rotten orange sequentially instead of a single simultaneous multi-source BFS, producing an incorrect (inflated) minute count
Forgetting to track and check the remaining fresh orange count, missing the -1 impossible case
Off-by-one errors in counting minutes, e.g., incrementing the counter even for an empty final level
Not correctly initializing all rotten oranges into the BFS queue simultaneously at minute 0, treating them as separate sequential sources instead

problems.name: Longest Common Subsequence
problems.description: Given two strings text1 and text2, return the length of their longest common subsequence, or 0 if no common subsequence exists. A subsequence is a sequence derived from a string by deleting some or no characters without changing the relative order of the remaining characters. A common subsequence of two strings is a subsequence that appears in both of them.
constraints: text1 and text2 consist of only lowercase English characters

examples.explanation: The longest common subsequence is "ace", with length 3.
The entire string is a common subsequence of itself.
There are no common characters at all, so the longest common subsequence has length 0.

edge_cases: No common characters at all (result is 0)
One string is a subsequence of the other entirely
Both strings identical
Single character strings
Strings with many repeated characters requiring careful DP transitions

hidden_test_cases.reason: Catches performance issues or off-by-one errors at maximum input size with maximal overlap
Catches implementations that incorrectly assume any character overlap contributes more than it validly can given strict order preservation
Catches base case handling for empty or near-empty inputs, verifying dp table initialization correctness

hints: Think about comparing the strings character by character from the start, and consider what happens when characters match versus when they don't.
Define dp[i][j] as the length of the longest common subsequence between the first i characters of text1 and the first j characters of text2.
If text1[i-1] equals text2[j-1], you can extend the LCS found without those two characters by 1; otherwise, take the best of skipping a character from either string.

solution_approach.key_observation: The longest common subsequence of two prefixes can be built from the longest common subsequences of slightly shorter prefixes, branching on whether the final characters of each prefix match.
solution_approach.algorithm: Create a 2D DP table of size (text1.length + 1) x (text2.length + 1), initialized to 0 along the first row and column (representing empty-string comparisons). For each i from 1 to text1.length and each j from 1 to text2.length: if text1[i-1] == text2[j-1], set dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j-1] + 1; otherwise, set dp[i][j] = max(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1]). The final answer is dp[text1.length][text2.length].
solution_approach.why_it_works: When the current characters match, they can always be included in an optimal common subsequence, extending the best solution found without them; when they don't match, the best solution must come from ignoring one character or the other, and taking the maximum of those two options correctly captures every possibility.
solution_approach.implementation_notes: The DP table can be space-optimized to use only two rows (the current and previous row) instead of the full 2D table, reducing space from O(m*n) to O(min(m,n)), since each row only depends on the row directly above it.

problems.expected_time_complexity: O(m * n) where m and n are the lengths of the two strings
problems.expected_space_complexity: O(m * n) for the full DP table (reducible to O(min(m,n)) with row-rolling optimization)
problems.what_you_learn: The classic 2D dynamic programming pattern for comparing two sequences, foundational for a wide range of string comparison and edit-distance-style problems.
common_mistakes: Off-by-one errors between the DP table's 1-indexed convention and the strings' 0-indexed characters
Forgetting to initialize the first row and column to 0, representing comparisons against an empty string
Confusing 'subsequence' (order preserved, characters can be non-contiguous) with 'substring' (must be contiguous), leading to an incorrect algorithm
Using recursion without memoization, causing exponential time complexity on longer strings
